title: Tolkien's Guide to Living Through Dark Times
author: The Culturist
summary: The Culturist explores how J.R.R. Tolkien's Lord of the Rings—begun in the WWI trenches—offers a framework for preserving creative and moral vitality in the face of overwhelming darkness. The key contrast is between Denethor's doom-laden capitulation and Samwise Gamgee's capacity to hold onto beauty and goodness even at the edge of annihilation. Proximity to evil does not determine whether a person succumbs to despair; what matters is what they cultivate within themselves when all external hope has failed.
points: Tolkien began his epic from the WWI trenches, one of the darkest possible creative conditions, yet produced work that has sustained readers through their own dark times for nearly a century.
Denethor's doomerism does not result from greater proximity to evil than Samwise's; the difference lies in what each character chooses to hold in their heart when all appears lost.
Samwise's glimpse of a white star above Mordor's cloud becomes a symbol of internal goodness preserved when all external conditions point toward despair and surrender.
The art that emerges from dark hours is itself revelatory: those who cling to beautiful thoughts in dark times can withstand tribulations that destroy those who have already surrendered hope.

Homer witnessed the most brutal acts of Bronze Age warfare yet turned them into the foundational work of Western literature—suggesting the capacity to create beauty outlasts its surrounding conditions.
quotes: Homer, author of the Iliad, witnessed the most brutal acts of Bronze Age warfare (as you can tell from the descriptive manner in which his war poetry is written), yet turned them into a tale of virtue that became the foundational work of Western literature.

Before examining why this mindset is wrong in the eyes of Tolkien, consider first the perspective of another… The Light Beyond Reach After passing into Mordor and escaping the orc tower at Cirith Ungol, Frodo and Sam are physically and spiritually depleted.

At the edge of all things, the star is a symbol of the goodness Samwise clings to within his own heart, and this sustains him to the very end of his quest — but what provides a person the determination to cling on?
One of the most quoted and uplifting passages of the entire novel follows: There, peeping among the cloud-wrack above a dark tor high up in the mountains, Sam saw a white star twinkle for a while.
In the case of The Lord of the Rings, we see that those characters who hang onto beautiful thoughts in dark times can withstand virtually any tribulation — but how do they manage it?
Proximity to evil is not the explanation for Denethor’s “doomerism.” But why, then, is Samwise able to cultivate beautiful thoughts at the brink of annihilation and Denethor is not?
